outcome: No verified mathematical progress on the Erdős–Oler conjecture was found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains proven only for n ≤ 15 (Payan 1997), and the only candidate development is an unrefereed, un-peer-reviewed document circulating on academia.edu and ResearchGate that claims a full proof but cannot be verified.
summary: The Erdős–Oler conjecture (packing n−1 vs. n circles in an equilateral triangle when n is triangular) is still listed by Wikipedia's 'Circle packing in an equilateral triangle' article as proven only for n ≤ 15 (Payan, 1997), with no citations after 2000 and no indication of recent progress; I fetched this article directly and it shows no 2024–2026 update. The only candidate development in the window is a document titled 'Optimal Circle Packings for Triangular Numbers: A Detailed Mathematical Proof [of/For] the Erdős-Oler Conjecture,' posted to academia.edu (accessed with a posting/scrape date around June 2025) and reposted to ResearchGate (search snippets place it around December 2024). I was unable to open either page directly — both academia.edu and ResearchGate returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches — and could not find the author's name, an abstract, or any secondary discussion, citation, review, or rebuttal of it anywhere else (no MathOverflow, Reddit, blog, or arXiv trace; it has never been posted to arXiv). Search results describe it only as 'self-published,' with no clear authorship or evidence of expert scrutiny. Because I could not read the argument, could not confirm it is a genuine mathematical proof rather than promotional or AI-generated text, and found no expert or community engagement with it, it does not meet even the `claimed` bar (which requires a genuine, identifiable preprint or announcement), let alone `resolved`. I also confirmed that an unrelated widely-reported 2026 AI mathematics story — a 23-year-old amateur using ChatGPT to resolve the Erdős primitive-set conjecture on 'primitive sets' — is a different Erdős conjecture entirely and has no bearing on Erdős–Oler. I therefore classify this as `open` with `no_change_found` true, while flagging the self-published document as an unresolved loose end rather than asserting nothing at all exists.
competing_reading: If the self-published academia.edu/ResearchGate document is in fact a legitimate, correct proof authored by a real mathematician, this record understates progress — it would potentially warrant `claimed`. The triage record and my own searches could not confirm or refute this because the hosting sites blocked automated access and no independent source has engaged with the document's content, author, or claims.
what_would_settle_it: Direct (manual, logged-in or archived) access to the academia.edu/ResearchGate document to identify its author and read the actual argument; any citation of it in a peer-reviewed venue, on arXiv, or by a recognized discrete-geometry researcher (e.g. via Packomania, MathOverflow, or a specialist blog); or an update to the Wikipedia article's stated bound (n ≤ 15) reflecting new verified cases.
